Re: Downtown Lewiston Redevelopment Plan and Tax Increment Financing District 
Dear Members of City Council: 
The Economic Development Team is pleased to submit the following downtown Lewiston map for the 
proposed City of Lewiston Downtown Redevelopment Plan and Downtown Tax Increment Financing 
District. 
A critical component of this process is defining Lewiston's downtown. The proposed map, Exhibit A, 
was developed with influence from prior city planning documents, including: 
• 1999 Downtown Master Plan 
• 2002 Downtown Housing Study 
• 2004 Downtown Streetscape Study 
• 2017 Comprehensive Plan (Legacy Lewiston) 
• 2025 Downtown Architectural Survey 
Economic Development staff also discussed the proposed map with city staff from Planning & Code 
Enforcement and Administration, as well LaRochelle Consulting, the city's TIF consultant, and staff at 
the Maine Department of Economic and Community Development. The proposed Downtown map 
reflects input from these conversations. 
The proposed map outlines an area that begins to the southeast of the Riverfront Island (Gully Brook), 
includes the Blanchard Mill and Lewiston DP W, runs along Blake Street to Main Street, up to Holland 
Street, with the northern edge along Holland and Avon Street. The proposed district runs along the 
Androscoggin river, including the Riverfront Island, down to its southern edge at Gully Brook. 
The proposed downtown area covers approximately 342 acres. Nearly 29.5 of those acres are in existing 
TIF districts and therefore would not be included in the Downtown Omnibus T IF. 
The city is required to create a Downtown Redevelopment Plan as part of the process for developing the 
Downtown Omnibus TIF District. The process for creating the Redevelopment Plan and Omnibus TIF 
District is as follows: 
1. Define the Downtown area 
1. Build consensus through conversation and review with City staff and City Council 
2. Compile materials for Downtown Redevelopment Plan, which outlines the city' s vision for 
downtown Lewiston. A full list of criteria for the plan is contained within Exhibit B. 
3. Hold multiple discussions/updates on the Redevelopment Plan with stakeholders, including 
DLA, Metro Chamber of Commerce, Lewiston Planning Board and Tag

during the second City Council meeting in February. Once approved, the plan will be sent to the 
Maine Department of Economic and Community Development 
5· Develop the Downtown Omnibus TIF District, incorporating much of the work done for the 
Redevelopment Plan 
6. Hold an executive session with City Council on the Downtown Omnibus TIF 
7· Present the Downtown TIF Omnibus to City Council for approval at a public hearing. Once 
approved, the TIF application will be sent to DECD by March 1, 2027 
The Downtown Redevelopment Plan defines the city' s vision for the physical and economic 
development of downtown Lewiston, incorporating data on existing infrastructure, buildings, and 
economic opportunities. As mentioned, the full criteria for the Downtown Redevelopment Plan is 
contained in Exhibit B. 
Determining the boundaries of Lewiston's downtown is the first critical step in this process and once an 
area has been outlined, Economic Development will begin the process of building the Downtown 
Redevelopment Plan and the Downtown Omnibus TIF. 
CONCLUSION 
The proposed Downtown map is the result of staff input informed by the City's existing planning 
documents. It is intended to be the first key piece in Economic Development's work to develop a 
Downtown Omnibus TIF District that will support investment and development in Lewiston. We look 
forward to working with City Council, Planning & Code Enforcement, Public Works, and Lewiston 
residents and stakeholders to ensure that this process results in a cohesive community vision and plan for 
the downtown area

components. Ensure your municipal Downtown Redevelopment Plan has the following components.

SUBJECT:  
Amendment to the Traffic Schedule to prohibit parking on a portion of Brann Avenue. 
 
  
INFORMATION: 
On September 28, 2026 LPW and LPD met with 2 property owners on Brann Ave to discuss parking issues. 
The owners explained that the current situation of allowing parking on both sides of the streets has created 
problems for accessing their driveways. They showed how when large vehicles park on the south side of 
Brann Ave that it creates difficulty for accessing the driveways on the North Side. LPW recently repaved 
this section of road and in doing so added a concrete curb to the south side to assist with water runoff. This 
newly installed curb has made the existing problem worse, and it does not allow vehicles to partially pull off 
the road when parking on this side. In speaking with LPW, they agree that street parking on the narrow 
street does create challenges when plowing. Also, if vehicles were to park on both sides of the road, as is 
now allowed, the road would be significantly reduced and for larger vehicles would only be a single lane 
road.  
In order to address these issues, LPW and LPD recommend adding the below section:  
Section 9 
Brann Ave- Odd numbered side, south side, starting at the intersection of East Ave and continuing east for 
315 feet. 
 
The Lewiston Police Department and the Lewiston Public Works Department are in support of this 
amendment to the Traffic Schedule.  
 
 
 
APPROVAL AND/OR COMMENTS OF CITY ADMINISTRATOR: 
 
The City Administrator recommends approval of the requested action.

One of the most powerful collection tools in a municipality’s arsenal is the ability to lien properties 
for delinquent taxes (real and sp ecial only), water, sewer, and  storm water balances. Once a lien is 
recorded, eighteen months must lapse without payment before the  lien matures. Prior to maturity, 
the City Council may waive the right to foreclose on a maturing lien as you have done in the past. If 
the lien is permitted to mature, the municipality may elect to foreclose on the property or, if 
subsequent payment is received, return the property to its owner via a quitclaim deed. 
 
At this time, the Finance Dir ector is asking the Council to approve a municipal quitclaim deed for 
the property located at the above listed location. The quitclaim deed will release any interest the City 
may have by virtue of undischarg ed real estate tax liens or utility liens on these properties. 
Payments due for this property have all been received in full. Should the Council approve this Order,

Re: Tax Lien Foreclosure Waivers 
 
Tax liens and water, sewer, and stormwater liens automatically mature 18 months following the 
ﬁling of a lien on a property by the City.  At that point, the City assumes technical ownership.  
The matured lien provides the City leverage to recover back taxes with interest as well as 
delinquent utility balances with late fees.  In the vast majority of cases, amounts owed the City 
are eventually paid and the property is “quit claimed” back to the owner.  In some cases, the City 
is paid when the property’s title must be cleared so it can be sold.  In infrequent and unusual 
cases, the City may take possession and sell the structure (or the property after a structure is 
removed) to recover amounts owed or to allow for redevelopment.  In isolated cases, however, 
the owner may simply abandon the property and walk away.  This generally occurs when the 
value of the property is less than the amounts owed or where signi ﬁcant liabilities are associated 
with the property, such as the presence of hazardous waste or materials.  Where a matured lien 
is in place and a property has been abandoned for a period of 60 days or more, the City 
potentially assumes certain liabilities associated with the property, including those arising from 
any injuries that might occur on the property.  Full City ownership of and liability for such 
structures can, therefore, arise without the City making a conscious determination that it should 
do so.    
Inadvertent assumption of unrecoverable liabilities is most likely to occur when liens mature on 
structures located on leased-land where the cost to remove an abandoned, blighted, and/or 
condemned structure falls on the City with little chance of either recovering the costs associated 
with demolition or seeing the beneﬁts of redevelopment (since the land on which these 
structures are located is under separate ownership and generally non-conforming as to our land 
development code). Such structures can include trailers and mobile homes in parks throughout 
the City as well as permanent structures such as those located in the Lincoln Street area.   In 
these cases, the City may also be exposed to the requirement of paying rental fees to the owner 
of the land on which the structure is located.  
The City may avoid these problems by waiving foreclosure, a process that requires a simple vote 
by the City Council.   
As has been the case for many years, staff have reviewed the structures located on leased land 
which have tax liens maturing on December 24, 2026.  In those instances where the structures
appear to be in poor or worse condition, we are recommending that foreclosure be waived to 
avoid City assumption of costs and liabilities and where it is unlikely that the City would recover 
costs associated with securing and/or demolishing these structures. 
This year, we are recommending that foreclosure be waived on thirty-three structures on leased 
land.

Purpose 
 
During the recent City Council workshop on solid waste services, the Council expressed consensus for 
an immediate interim measure to restore municipal collection for small, owner-occupied mixed-use 
properties that previously received city trash pickup prior to recent route adjustments.  
 
This memorandum provides a brief overview of the draft amendment to Chapter ൦ൢ (Solid Waste), 
outlines the rationale for limiting eligibility to properties with up to three residential units, and identifies 
the specific sections of the code where these revisions appear.  
 
Overview of Proposed Amendments 
 
The proposed amendment establishes a targeted exception to the general prohibition against collecting 
waste from properties with commercial activities. Under this change, qualifying "live-work" 
properties—where a local business owner maintains their primary legal domicile on-site—can resume 
standard municipal curbside collection.  
The amendment establishes the following qualifying standards: 
• Unit Threshold: The property must contain no more than three (3) residential dwelling units, 
regardless of the number of commercial units on the parcel.  
• Verified Owner-Occupancy: The property owner must reside in one of the on-site residential 
units as their primary legal residence, verified through Assessing records, an active Homestead 
Exemption, or a valid state-issued ID.  
• Cart Allotment & Waste Limits: Service is limited to one city-issued rolling cart for the 
owner-occupied unit, plus one cart per tenant residential unit up to the program limit. Collected 
waste must consist of standard household-type solid waste; any commercial waste must be non-
hazardous, non-industrial, and fit inside the authorized carts with lids closed.  
• Prior Service Connection: Eligible properties must have historically received municipal pickup 
prior to the automated cart rollout or had service discontinued solely due to the commercial 
activity classification of the building.
Rationale for the Three-Unit Ceiling 
Staff specifically structured this interim exception for properties containing one to three residential 
dwelling units to align with the city's existing residential framework:  
• Parity with Existing Residential Rules: Under Chapter 62, Section 62-11, the current definition 
of Residential properties already provides standard, tax-funded municipal pickup to three-unit 
buildings (triplexes), provided that one of the units is occupied by the property owner.  
• Preventing Policy Inconsistencies: Setting the mixed-use residential ceiling at three units 
creates policy consistency between pure multi-family buildings and mixed-use buildings. A 
mixed-use building owner living on-site above a small shop will receive the same residential 
service access as a resident living in an owner-occupied triplex.  
• Preserving Council Direction for the Full Overhaul: While the broader proposal presented at 
the workshop contemplates a universal four-unit collection ceiling across all property types, that 
change involves larger operational and fee-structure adjustments. Maintaining a three-unit 
threshold for this interim amendment provides immediate relief to affected resident shopkeepers 
without prematurely altering the baseline multi-family definitions ahead of the upcoming 
comprehensive ordinance rewrite. 
Location of Changes in Draft Ordinance 
The proposed revisions appear as underlined text in two locations within the attached draft of Chapter 
62:  
1. Chapter 62, Section 62-11 (Definitions) – Page 1: 
Adds the formal definition of Owner-occupied mixed-use property: 
"Any parcel of property located within the city containing one or more commercial units or non-
residential commercial activities and containing not more than three (3) residential dwelling 
units, where at least one (1) of the residential dwelling units is continuously occupied by the 
record property owner as their primary legal residence." 
2. Chapter 62, Section 62-13(b)(7) (Curbside Collection Exception) – Page 3: 
Inserts subsection (7) Exception for Owner-Occupied Mixed-Use Properties (1 to 3 Residential Units) 
directly following the existing provisions governing multi-unit service. This subsection codifies 
the unit cap, residency verification, cart allocations, allowable waste character, and historical 
service requirements.  
Staff are available to answer any questions regarding this language prior to or during the upcoming

Sec. 23-300.- Purpose 
The purpose of this ordinance is to protect residents living in mobile home parks 
from unreasonable lot rent and fee increases. Many mobile home residents own their 
mobile home and rent a mobile home park lot.  Mobile homes can be difficult and 
expensive to move from one parcel of land to another.  Mobile home parks represent a 
source of unsubsidized affordable housing, and mobile home park residents are 
particularly vulnerable to unreasonable rent and fee increases. This ordinance establishes a 
review process to ensure that rent and fee increases ar e reasonably tied to increases in the 
Consumer Price Index and a mobile home park’s increased costs in maintaining and 
improving the park.

meaning:

owner demands of a mobile home resident, or that a mobile home resident pays to a park owner. 
Additional fees may include a capital expense. 
Administrator means the municipal official responsible for the administration and 
enforcement of this mobile home park rent stabilization ordinance. The Administrator shall be 
the City Administrator or the City Administrator‘s designee. 
Base Rent means the total amount of rent and fees charged by a park owner for any

may include a capital expense. 
Capital expense means any expenditure made by a park owner to fund the cost of a 
capital improvement.

functionality of the park as a whole, or (3) adds a new amenity or facility.

Sec. 23-303.- Base Rent and Additional Fees Increase Limitations for mobile home parks 
owned by large institutional investors.  
(a) Applicability.  This section shall apply to a park owner that is a large institutional 
investor. 
(b) Base Rent.  A large institutional investor shall not demand, accept or retain base rent 
for a mobile home park lot that exceeds the base rent as provided for herein.  
(1) The amount of a base rent increase for a prospective period shall be determined 
by multiplying the current base rent by the maximum annual increase or a lesser 
amount. 
(2) A park owner may increase base rent whenever a lawful vacancy occurs, and this 
amount shall be considered the new base rent for that mobile home park lot 
without a requirement to petition the rent stabilization board. Any new base rent 
set pursuant to this paragraph shall be subject to all limitations, formulas, and 
procedural requirements for future base rent increases contained in this section. 
(c) Additional Fees: Except as provided herein, a park owner shall not demand, accept 
or retain additional fees that exceed the additional fees on the effective date of this 
ordinance. A park owner that seeks to impose a new or increased additional fee shall 
petition and obtain advance approval for the fee from the rent stabilization board. 
(d) Petition for Increase In Base Rent, Greater Than the Maximum Annual 
Increase, or Additional Fees: A park owner seeking to increase base rent, greater 
than the maximum annual increase, or additional fees must submit a petition to the 
rent stabilization board. A park owner may seek an increase in base rent, greater than 
the maximum annual increase, or additional fees because of the cost of increased 
operating expenses such as taxes, insurance, utility charges and maintenance costs; 
and/or the cost of capital expenses, in excess of those accounted for in the base rent, 
that directly benefit mobile home residents.   
(1) The complete petition must be filed more than 157 days prior to the effective date 
of the proposed increase and contain documentation that the increase is necessary 
to cover increased operating expenses or the cost of eligible capital 
improvements.  The petition shall include a petition fee, in accordance with the 
schedule as established by the city council. 
(2) The city clerk shall determine whether the petition is complete.  If the 
Administrator determines that a submitted petition is not complete, the petitioner 
shall be notified within fourteen (14) days after receipt of the petition of the 
additional information required to process the petition. If such additional 
information is not submitted within thirty (30) days of the city clerk’s request, or

such later time that the city clerk provides, the petition shall be deemed to be 
denied. If the city clerk determines the application is complete, the city clerk shall 
notify the petitioner and the rent stabilization board. 
(3) Standards:  
a. Standard for petition based on increased operating expenses: A park 
owner petitioning for a base rent increase in excess of the maximum 
annual increase or an additional fees increase based in whole or in part on 
increased operating expenses must demonstrate to the rent stabilization 
board that there are actual and reasonable operating expenses in excess of 
the maximum annual increase allowed that are necessary to maintain the 
existing level of services to the mobile home park residents or that are 
necessary to implement an increase in services that will have a direct 
benefit to the mobile home park residents. 
b. Standard for petition based on increased eligible capital expenses: A 
park owner petitioning for a base rent increase in excess of the maximum 
annual increase or an additional fee increase based in whole or in part on 
increased eligible capital expenses must demonstrate to the rent 
stabilization board: 
(1) That the capital improvement will have a direct benefit to the 
mobile home park residents;  
(2) The total capital outlay required for the capital improvement;  
(3) The useful life of the capital improvement, as determined by 
generally accepted accounting principles or IRS depreciation 
schedules;

the improvement calculated as the prevailing yield on ten-year 
U.S. Treasury securities plus two (2) percentage points, as

(5) The proposed base rent or additional fee increase calculated as the

divided by the useful life of the capital improvement divided by 
the number of sites in the mobile home park specified in the park’s 
license issued pursuant to 10 M.R.S. §9082 of the Manufactured 
Housing Act.  
c. Additional Standard for a petition for an additional fee increase.  A 
park owner seeking an additional fee increase shall have the additional 
burden of demonstrating to the rent stabilization board:

and

Pursuant to ൣൠ-A M.R.S. § ൢൡൠൣ, the Charter Commission will consist of nine members, including six
